title: git reset --hard wiped a day of uncommitted work
intro: A teammate ran 'git reset --hard' to 'clean things up' and lost a day's work that was never committed. The reflog shows nothing useful, because there was no commit. But they remember running 'git add src/pricing.py' a few hours ago, before making more edits.

steps.prompt: Check the reflog anyway, to confirm there's no commit holding the work.
steps.fake_output:
b7c8d9e HEAD@{0}: reset: moving to HEAD
b7c8d9e HEAD@{1}: pull: Fast-forward
3e1f0a9 HEAD@{2}: checkout: moving from feature/tax to main
steps.hint: git reflog shows HEAD's movements; uncommitted work never appears in it.

steps.prompt: 'git add' wrote the file's contents into the object database even though it was never committed. Search for objects nothing points to.
steps.fake_output:
Checking object directories: 100% (256/256), done.
dangling blob 6e2f9a1c4b8d7e3f0a5c2b9d8e7f6a5b4c3d2e1f
dangling blob a4c1e8f27b3d9065c2e4f6a8b0d1c3e5f7a9b2d4
dangling commit 1d2e3f4a5b6c7d8e9f0a1b2c3d4e5f6a7b8c9d0e
steps.hint: git fsck --lost-found lists 'dangling' objects: stored, but unreachable from any branch.

steps.prompt: Two dangling blobs. Look at the first one, 6e2f9a1c, to see whether it's the pricing file.
steps.fake_output:
"""Pricing rules for the checkout flow."""

def price_with_tax(order, region):
    base = order.subtotal_cents
    rate = TAX_RATES[region]
    ...
steps.hint: git cat-file -p <sha> prints an object's contents.

steps.prompt: That's it. Write the blob 6e2f9a1c back to src/pricing.py.
steps.fake_output: (no output: src/pricing.py restored as it was when it was staged)
steps.hint: Redirect the object's contents into the file.

steps.prompt: Commit it straight away so it's safe, as a work-in-progress commit.
expected_commands: git add src/pricing.py && git commit -m "wip: pricing rules"
git add src/pricing.py && git commit -m 'wip: pricing rules'
steps.fake_output:
[main 2c3d4e5] wip: pricing rules
 1 file changed, 64 insertions(+), 12 deletions(-)
steps.hint: git add the file and commit.

resolution: 'git reset --hard' discards uncommitted changes, and the reflog can't help because the reflog tracks commits. The save came from a detail of how Git works: 'git add' writes a blob into the object database immediately. Staging a file is enough to store its contents, and unreferenced objects live for about two weeks before garbage collection removes them. So the version that was staged was recoverable; the edits made after that last 'git add' were never given to Git and are gone for good (an editor's local history is the only other hope). The lasting lessons: commit early and often, since a WIP commit costs nothing and can be squashed later; prefer 'git stash' to 'reset --hard' when you want a clean tree; and remember this trick, because 'I ran reset --hard' is one of the most common Git emergencies and it's often partly recoverable.
